chapter: Al Hibbler, Dakota Staton and later years
title: Joining Al Hibbler, whose Unchained Melody and He make the best money
summary: Hibbler calls him in late 1954; hits like Unchained Melody and He in 1955-56 bring his highest salaries.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Anyway, late in 1954, I got this call from Al Hibbler in New York, telling me that he had just recorded an album, and he was going out on his own, and he would like for me to travel with him as his pianist. And I'd known Al from a long time back, from the days in Chicago, the Trummy Young days. We had been friends through the years and everything. So it was always a pleasure to work with Al. He and I always had a
lot of fun together. So I decided I would go and work with him.

And it turned out to be a very successful thing. I worked with him, and the end result was that I ended up making more money with Al than I did with anyone I had ever worked. I got paid the highest salaries that I'd ever been paid with Al Hibbler. The reason was that in the year of 1955, he had his first big hit came through, and it was a thing called "The Unchained Melody." Following that, he had another hit, a thing called "He." He received gold records for both of these things, I think. Then the following year, I believe, he had a hit with this thing called "After the Lights Go Down Low," which was a kind of funny blues sounding thing, but it was a very, very big record for him. And he had these three big records...
